e: From Afrikaans mielie, from Portuguese milho.
From French mine (“appearance”) (whence also Danish mine and German Miene), perhaps from Breton min (“face of an animal”), or from Latin minio (“to redden”).
q: Gentlest Guardians marked serene / His early hope, his liberal mien; […]
1847, R[alph] W[aldo] Emerson, “Threnody”, in Poems, Boston, Mass.: James Munroe and Company, →OCLC, page 238:

Beauty, like all divine gifts, is everywhere to be seen by the eye of the faithful admirer of nature; and, like all spirits, she is scarcely to be described by words. Her countenance and mien, her path, her hue and carriage, often surpass expression, and soothe the enthusiast into reverie and silence.
1856, Joseph Turnley, The Language of the Eye, →OCLC, page 111:
Jenny's coming o'er the green, / Fairer form was never seen, / Winning is her gentle mien; / Why do I love her so?
1860, Stephen Foster, “Jenny's coming o'er the green”:
[T]aking the air with an infinite sadness of mien, like some disconsolate prisoner, Utterson saw Dr. Jekyll.
1886 January 5, Robert Louis Stevenson, “Incident at the Window”, in Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., →OCLC, page 63:
He could remain a useful White House counselor — no mieskeit, he — but he would not be a credible Attorney General.
1984 March 30, William Safire, “The Meese Mess”, in The New York Times, page A31:
Then he would pretend to call to my mother who was busy in the kitchen making breakfast, to come up and see me, to look at what a mieskeit her daughter was in the morning.
2012, Fern Kupfer, chapter 4, in Leaving Long Island and other departures, Ames, IA: Culicidae Press, →ISBN, page 40:
Much more helpful than the press trip was the performance of an icy-miened 14-year-old Romanian gymnast, Nadia Comaneci.
2010, Tom Mackin, Making Other Plans: A Memoir, page 236:
